---
title: "What Is Worth Building"
---

## Why This Matters

Building is cheap now, so the expensive mistake is building the wrong thing. Before you can
build well, you have to decide what deserves to exist. This chapter is the Aim end of the
loop: whether there is a real problem worth solving, where you will compete and how you mean to win, how a product
creates and captures value, and whether the thing you are considering is good for the people
who will use it. Those belong together: a product that solves no real problem, cannot hold
any of the value it creates, or harms the people who use it has failed the same test.

<!-- learn -->

## Why Most Products Fail

CB Insights reads the post-mortems of failed startups and tallies the reasons founders give. Its
March 2026 analysis covered 431 venture-backed companies that shut down since 2023. "Ran out of
capital" topped the list at 70%, followed by poor product-market fit (the product did not meet a
need that enough customers would pay for) at 43%, bad timing at 29%,
and unsustainable unit economics (each customer cost more to win and serve than they paid) at 19% (most companies cited more than one reason)
[@cbinsights2026]. The report adds an interpretation: running out of money is almost
always the last event in a failure and rarely its cause. The money ran out because the product did not fit a market
that wanted it badly enough to pay.

For a builder, poor product-market fit means a team spent its runway (the money and months it had before the money ran out) building
something too few people needed. That mistake gets easier when an agent can build an
app in an afternoon: you can now build the wrong thing faster than before.

This happens because of what we call **The Idea Trap**: falling in love with a solution before understanding the problem. It looks like this:

> "I have a great idea for an app that does X!"

That statement starts with a solution. You've already decided what to build before asking whether anyone needs it. This is backwards.

<!-- learn -->

## Problem vs. Solution Thinking

**The model:** a real problem exists without your product. Describe it so that a person who has
never heard your idea would recognize it from their own life.

That one-line test, call it the **stranger test**, separates the two kinds of statement:

- A **solution statement** names a thing to build. Only someone who has heard your pitch can
  agree or disagree with it.
- A **problem statement** names a person, a situation, and what goes wrong for them today. A
  stranger who lives it says "yes, that happens to me," and one who does not says "no, it
  doesn't," which is just as useful.

**Solution thinking** starts with technology or features:

- "Let's build an AI-powered calendar app"
- "We should make a blockchain-based voting system"
- "What if we created a social network for pet owners?"

**Problem thinking** starts with pain:

- "Professionals who meet with outside clients lose time to email back-and-forth just to find a meeting slot"
- "Voters distrust election integrity and want verifiable results"
- "Pet owners struggle to find trustworthy sitters when they travel"

The difference looks small and has large consequences. Solution thinking leads you to build features. Problem thinking leads you to understand customers.

**A worked example.** A student starts with "an AI app that builds study schedules." That fails the
stranger test: nobody has an AI-study-schedule problem. Strip out the product and ask what happens
today: "Students taking five classes find out a big assignment is due tomorrow because the due
dates live in five different Canvas courses and syllabi." A stranger can check that against their
own week. It also opens answers the original idea would have hidden: a calendar export, a weekly
email, a habit of checking one page. Some of those need no AI at all.

A quick check you can run on any statement: if it contains an app, a feature, a technology, or the
words "a way to," it is probably a solution statement.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
Rewrite each of these so it mentions no product, feature, or technology, only a person, a
situation, and what goes wrong:

1. "An app that splits the bill at dinner."
2. "A Slack bot that reminds my team about standups."
3. "AI that writes cover letters."
4. "A marketplace for renting textbooks."
5. "A dashboard for club treasurers."

Then run the stranger test on your own current idea. If your rewrite still only makes sense to
someone who has heard your pitch, you have not found the problem yet. You can ask Claude to
critique your rewrites, but tell it to flag any word that implies a solution.
:::

<!-- learn -->

## Vision before strategy

Before the strategy comes a **product vision**: a description of the better world your product creates, usually a few years out. Marty Cagan argues the vision is what recruits people, aligns decisions, and keeps a team going through the difficult middle of the work [@cagan2017inspired]. Strategy is how you get there; vision is the destination and the reason to go. Write the vision first, then let the strategy serve it.

<!-- learn -->

## Strategy is choosing what not to do

Michael Porter's foundational point: the essence of strategy is choosing what *not* to do [@porter1996strategy]. Strategy is a small set of hard choices that fit together, which you then defend against the constant temptation to do everything. A list of every good thing you could do does not qualify. If your "strategy" contains no sacrifices, it is a wish list.

<!-- learn -->

## Where to play, and how to win

Roger Martin and A.G. Lafley (*Playing to Win*) [@lafley2013playing] reduce strategy to a cascade of five linked choices:

1. **What is your winning aspiration?** The purpose. What does winning look like?
2. **Where will you play?** Which customers, segments, channels. (Your beachhead, the narrow first customer in [Finding and Validating the Problem](04-finding-and-validating-the-problem.qmd), is a where-to-play choice.)
3. **How will you win?** Your source of advantage in that arena: cheaper, far better at one job, a network others cannot match.
4. **What capabilities must you have?** The few things you must be great at.
5. **What management systems are required?** How you keep it running.

For a student product, the first three matter most. Answer "where will you play" and "how will you win" in a sentence each, and you have written down more strategy than most startups do.

One thing has changed about "where will you play." The old advice was to chase a large market,
because the fixed cost of building was high enough that a small one could not repay it. That
arithmetic is different now.

::: tweet-center
<blockquote class="twitter-tweet">

<p lang="en" dir="ltr">

Software development has historically been constrained by scarcity, high costs, specialized skills, and long timelines. So builders chased only big markets.<br><br> AI is making it cheap, fast, and easy to build, suddenly it's economically sane to solve niche workflows for small…

</p>

— Madhu Guru (\@realmadhuguru) <a href="https://twitter.com/realmadhuguru/status/1953253968228040778?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 7, 2025</a>

</blockquote>


A market too small to be worth a funded team's time can be worth yours. That widens where you can
play. How you win is just as demanding as before.

<!-- learn -->

## Creating value, and capturing it

Strategy has to answer two different questions, and it is easy to collapse them into one. The first is whether your product *creates* value: is anyone better off for it existing? The second is whether you can *capture* any of that value: does enough of it come back to you to keep the business alive? They are separate questions, and a product can pass the first and fail the second.

Adam Brandenburger and Harborne Stuart formalized this, defining value created as willingness to pay minus willingness to sell [@brandenburger1996]. **Willingness to pay** is the most a customer would pay for your product before walking away. **Willingness to sell** is the least a supplier would accept to provide what you need to make it, including your own time. Felix Oberholzer-Gee later turned that into the diagram now commonly used to teach it, the value stick [@oberholzergee2021]. At the top sits the customer's willingness to pay. At the bottom sits the cost of what you use to build, your suppliers' and your own willingness to sell. The gap between them is the value your product *creates*. How that gap gets divided, how much the customer keeps as a good deal, how much suppliers take, and how much is left for you, is the value you *capture*.

![The value stick. The whole height, willingness to pay down to willingness to sell, is the value created. The two interior lines, Price and Cost, divide it into what the customer keeps, what you capture, and what suppliers keep. Raising willingness to pay or lowering willingness to sell makes the stick taller, which creates value. Price is the only interior line you partly set, and moving it shifts value between the customer and you, which changes how much you capture.](images/diagrams/ch03-value-stick.svg){#fig-value-stick fig-alt="A vertical bar. Its top edge is labeled willingness to pay, the most the customer would give, and its bottom edge willingness to sell, the least suppliers would take. Two interior lines, price (what you actually charge) near the top and cost (what the inputs cost you) near the bottom, split the bar into three bands: customer's delight at the top, bracketed as the value the customer keeps; your margin in the middle, the largest band and highlighted, bracketed as the value you capture; and supplier's surplus at the bottom, bracketed as the value the supplier keeps. A larger bracket on the right spans the whole bar and is labeled total value created." width="100%"}

**A worked example, with made-up numbers.** Take the due-date app from [Problem vs. Solution Thinking](#problem-vs.-solution-thinking). A student would pay at most $10 a month for it: that is the top of the stick. Your hosting provider would accept as little as $2 per user per month to run it: that is the bottom (to keep it simple, count your own time as free). The app creates $8 a month of value per user. Now set a price of $6, and suppose hosting actually charges you $3. The student keeps $4 ($10 minus $6), you capture $3 ($6 minus $3), and the hosting provider keeps $1 ($3 minus $2). The three shares add up to the $8 created.

The value stick is a diagram of standard economics. If you want the full derivation, how producer surplus, accounting profit, economic profit, and finance's return above the cost of capital are all one idea measured at different levels of detail, and how they connect up to willingness to pay, it is worked out in the appendix, [The Logic of Value](A1-logic-of-value.qmd).

A common mistake is to assume that creating value is the hard part and capture will follow. It does not. Peter Thiel gives an example: US airlines create enormous value and keep almost none of it, while a single search company creates less and keeps far more [@thiel2014]. David Teece made the same point about innovators decades earlier: you can invent something new, create real value, and watch imitators and the owners of the pieces you depend on capture all of it [@teece1986]. Creating value is necessary. It is not sufficient.

So where on the value stick do you land? That is a choice, but a *constrained* one. You do not simply decide to keep more of the gap. How much you can capture is set by industry structure you did not build and cannot change by deciding to, and the first job of strategy is to assess that structure accurately. Call the part of the stick between price and cost, your margin, the **band**. In [AIRE](01-building-with-ai-agents.qmd#the-loop-how-this-course-works) terms, the width of the band you can capture is something you *Inform* on, and where you position inside it is the *Aim*. Misjudging the band is an information failure. If you judge the band correctly and it is thin, you have made no mistake; you have learned that you should look for a different band.

Value comes in many kinds, and many of them are not functional. Bain's Elements of Value catalogs thirty
distinct kinds, stacked from functional at the base through emotional and life changing up to social
impact. The higher elements are harder to copy and are what people pay a premium for, but
they only count once the functional ones underneath are handled.

![Image source: Almquist, Senior, and Bloch, "The Elements of Value," Harvard Business Review, 2016](images/elements-of-value.png){fig-alt="A pyramid of thirty value elements in four tiers. The base tier, functional, holds elements such as saves time, simplifies, makes money, reduces risk, organizes, integrates, connects, reduces effort, avoids hassles, reduces cost, quality, variety, sensory appeal, and informs. Above it, emotional, holds reduces anxiety, rewards me, nostalgia, design and aesthetics, badge value, wellness, therapeutic value, fun and entertainment, attractiveness, and provides access. Above that, life changing, holds provides hope, self-actualization, motivation, heirloom, and affiliation and belonging. The single top element is self-transcendence, under social impact."}

Use it as a checklist against your own product. If every element you can honestly claim sits in the
bottom row, you are competing on cost and convenience alone, which is the easiest position to copy.

<!-- learn -->

## The five forces: how wide is the band?

What sets the width of the band? Michael Porter's five forces [@porter1979competitive], read this way, are a diagnostic of exactly that: how much of the value an industry creates it will actually let you keep. In economic terms, the underlying variable is market power. Perfect competition drives price down to cost, hands the whole gap to customers, and leaves you almost nothing. Market power is what lets you hold price up toward willingness to pay and keep the gap.

The five forces measure that power at two points:

- **Rivalry, new entrants, and substitutes** decide whether the industry as a whole can hold price above cost, or whether competition and easy entry compete it away. For a new product the strongest substitute is usually the customer's current habit: the spreadsheet, the group text, or doing nothing.
- **Buyer power and supplier power** decide whether an adjacent player, a dominant customer or a must-have supplier, can bargain your share away even when the industry is otherwise attractive.

All five are the same variable, market power, at different points in the chain, held either by you or by someone else. One caution: the five forces describe how attractive the *industry* is, and say nothing about whether your product is the strongest in it. Two products in the same structure can capture very differently based on their own advantage, which is the subject of moats below.

![The five forces drawn on the value stick. Both sticks have the same willingness to pay and willingness to sell. Rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, and buyer power push price down; supplier power pushes cost up. Where the forces are strong, little of the stick is left as your margin. Five forces after Porter [-@porter1979competitive]; value stick after Oberholzer-Gee [-@oberholzergee2021].](images/diagrams/ch03-five-forces-band.svg){#fig-five-forces-band fig-alt="Two value sticks side by side, with the same willingness to pay at the top and the same willingness to sell at the bottom. Each stick is split by a Price line and a Cost line into customer's delight at the top, your margin in the middle, and supplier's surplus at the bottom. Under weak forces, price sits close to willingness to pay and cost sits close to willingness to sell, so your margin is most of the stick, and the two arrows pushing on price and cost are short. Under strong forces, a long arrow labeled rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, and buyer power pushes price down, and a long arrow labeled supplier power pushes cost up, so your margin is a thin band in the middle." width="100%"}

The two sticks create the same total value. The forces change only how it is divided: what the
forces push out of your margin goes to customers as a lower price or to suppliers as a higher
cost. Perfect competition is the limit case, where price is pushed all the way down to cost.

<!-- learn -->

## Blue oceans: widening the band

There is a third move, and it is the one to aim for. Instead of accepting the band the current industry allows and fighting for position inside it, you can redraw the boundary so you are measured against a different structure entirely. W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne call the crowded, well-mapped markets *red oceans*, where rivals compete for a fixed amount of demand, and the uncontested space you create *blue oceans*, where for a while there are no direct rivals, no established substitutes, and no one has entered yet [@kim2005blue]. The goal is to exit the existing competition.

Their method for this is *value innovation*: pursue differentiation and low cost at the same time instead of trading one for the other. On the value stick that means moving both ends at once, lifting willingness to pay while cutting cost, by dropping the factors your industry over-serves and adding factors it never offered. Cirque du Soleil cut the animals and star performers that made circuses expensive and added theatrical story and production that circuses never had, and landed in a space where neither circuses nor theater competed with it.

In AIRE this is discovery applied to the Aim instead of to the customer. Where the Mom Test (the customer-interview method in [Finding and Validating the Problem](04-finding-and-validating-the-problem.qmd)) informs you about needs *inside* a category, the blue ocean question informs you about where the category boundary could be *moved*: look across substitute industries, adjacent buyer groups, and complementary offerings for space no one is contesting. It is *Inform* in service of choosing a better place to play.

A blue ocean has an inherent problem, which the rest of this chapter addresses. By definition it has no barriers: you just created open space, which means entry is open to anyone. If you cannot build a reason for the space to stay yours, imitators enter, it becomes a red ocean, and your capture falls back toward zero. Creating the uncontested space is only half the move. Keeping it is the other half, which is Thiel's point: create a new market *and* own it. The first half is a blue ocean. The second is a moat.

![A blue ocean on the value stick. Value innovation raises willingness to pay and lowers willingness to sell at the same time, which makes the stick taller and leaves room for a wide margin. Without a moat, imitators enter and push price back down toward cost. With a moat, the margin stays wide. Blue ocean and value innovation from Kim and Mauborgne [-@kim2005blue].](images/diagrams/ch03-blue-ocean-moat.svg){#fig-blue-ocean-moat fig-alt="Four value sticks drawn on one scale, left to right. Red ocean: a short stick whose price and cost lines sit close together, so your margin is a thin band. An arrow labeled value innovation leads to Blue ocean: a taller stick whose top, willingness to pay, has moved up past the red ocean's top, marked add what the industry never offered, and whose bottom, willingness to sell, has moved down past the red ocean's bottom, marked drop what the industry over-serves. Its margin is wide. From the blue ocean, an arrow labeled imitators enter leads to Without a moat: the same tall stick, but price has fallen close to cost, which has not moved, and the margin is thin again. A curved arrow labeled imitators kept out leads over it to With a moat: the same tall stick with the same wide margin as the blue ocean." width="100%"}

<!-- learn -->

## Moats: why the win lasts

Winning once is not enough; the advantage has to last. Hamilton Helmer (*7 Powers*) [@helmer2016powers] catalogs the sources of durable advantage, or moats:

- **Network effects**: the product gets more valuable as more people use it; each new user improves it for the others.
- **Switching costs**: leaving is painful, so customers stay.
- **Scale economies**: you get cheaper per unit as you grow.
- **Brand**: trust and meaning competitors cannot quickly copy.
- **Counter-positioning**: a newcomer uses a better business model that established companies will not copy, because copying it would hurt the business they already have.
- **Cornered resource**: exclusive access to something valuable, such as a patent, key people, or data no one else has.
- **Process power**: ways of working, built up inside a company over years, that make its product better or cheaper and that others cannot copy quickly.

Ask honestly: once you are winning, what stops the next student with the same AI tools from copying you next week? If the answer is "nothing," you have a feature with no moat. With AI tools this question matters more than before, because copying costs less than it ever has. Strategy is largely the work of building an answer to it.

<!-- learn -->

## A test worth memorizing: DHM

Gibson Biddle, from leading product at Netflix, offers a compact test for a good product strategy: **DHM** [@biddle2018]. Does it **D**elight customers, in **H**ard-to-copy, **M**argin-enhancing ways? All three at once:

- **Delight**: customers love it; tolerating it does not count.
- **Hard to copy**: there is a moat, so the delight is defensible.
- **Margin-enhancing**: it improves the business's margins, beyond adding volume.

A product can delight and still lose (easily copied), or be defensible and still lose (nobody cares). DHM forces all three.

<!-- learn -->

## Putting it to work

Draft a one-page product strategy for your product:

- **Vision** (one paragraph): the better world you are building toward.
- **Where you play** (one sentence): your specific customer and beachhead.
- **How you win** (one sentence): your source of advantage.
- **Your moat** (one sentence): why the win lasts.
- **What you will NOT do** (a short list): the sacrifices.

Then pressure-test it with AI, but adversarially. Do not ask "is this a good strategy?", it will flatter you. Ask: "Attack this strategy. Where is the moat weakest? What would a competitor with the same AI tools do to beat it? What am I refusing to sacrifice that I should?" A strategy should survive that attack before competitors make it for real.

<!-- learn -->

## Understanding human nature cuts both ways

To build something people actually use, you have to understand how people actually work. Jonathan Haidt describes the mind as a small rider on a large elephant [@haidt2006happiness]. The rider is conscious reasoning. The elephant is emotion and habit: automatic, strong, and usually the one that decides where the two go. Daniel Kahneman draws the same split as a fast, automatic System 1 and a slow, deliberate System 2 [@kahneman2011thinking]. (The picture simplifies: the two are not separate parts of the brain, and the rider can train the elephant over time.) People also lean on mental shortcuts, accept defaults, and fall into habit loops. That knowledge is exactly what makes a product feel effortless and worth returning to.

![The rider (deliberate reasoning) can steer only when the elephant (emotion and intuition) is willing; when the two disagree, the elephant usually takes its own route. A product has to work for both, and the same understanding can be turned against the elephant. Adapted from Jonathan Haidt, *The Happiness Hypothesis* [@haidt2006happiness].](images/diagrams/ch03-rider-elephant.svg){#fig-rider-elephant fig-alt="A line drawing of a large elephant walking to the right with a small rider on its back holding the reins. The rider is labeled deliberate reasoning; the elephant is labeled emotion and intuition. Ahead of them the path forks. A dashed branch rising to the upper right is labeled route the rider chooses; a solid branch straight ahead is labeled route the elephant takes, and the elephant is walking onto the straight branch." width="100%"}

It is also exactly what makes a product manipulative. The same understanding of human defaults that lets you remove friction lets you engineer compulsion. The knowledge you are gaining in this class can produce a product that serves a person or one that exploits them. That is why the knowledge comes with a responsibility.

### Moral Foundations Theory

People are not blank slates about right and wrong. Research on moral foundations finds a handful of intuitions that recur across cultures: care versus harm, fairness versus cheating, loyalty, authority, sanctity, and liberty [@haidt2012righteous]. You need not adopt the theory wholesale to take its practical point: your users bring moral intuitions to your product, and they feel it when a product treats them unfairly, wastes them, or degrades them, even when they cannot name why. Building against those intuitions costs you trust, which is the one asset a product cannot fake.

### Hooked: engagement or exploitation

Habit-forming products run a loop: a trigger, an action, a variable reward (one that changes unpredictably each time, like new posts in a feed), and an investment (something the user puts in, such as data or followers, that brings them back) [@eyal2014hooked]. The mechanics are neutral. A fitness app and a slot machine use the same loop. The difference is entirely in the aim.

The honest test is simple: **would your user, in a calm and reflective moment, be glad you designed it this way?** A habit that helps someone do the thing they already want to do benefits them. A habit engineered to override their judgment and consume time they never meant to give is a harm, no matter how good the retention numbers look. This is where engagement metrics, the ones you will learn to track later in [Measuring What Matters](14-measuring-what-matters.qmd), can mislead you: engagement a user would disown on reflection is extraction, and it should not be counted as success.

### Algorithms and amplification

The moment your product recommends, ranks, or personalizes, it stops being a neutral tool and starts shaping what people see, want, and believe. An algorithm optimized purely for engagement will reliably discover that outrage, anxiety, and compulsion engage. If you build one, you own what it amplifies. Optimizing for a number without asking what that number does to a person is a moral decision, made by default when you decline to consider it.

<!-- learn -->

## Aiming well: virtue and the golden mean

If the aim is a question of values, it helps to be precise about what a good aim looks like. Aristotle gave the most influential answer [@aristotlenicomachean]. A virtue, he argued, is a **settled disposition to choose well**, as distinct from a feeling or a one-time act, and it lies in a **mean between two vices**: one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage is the mean between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity is the mean between stinginess and waste. His formal definition: virtue is "a state concerned with choice, lying in a mean relative to us, this being determined by reason." The vices are the two ways of missing.

That structure maps onto a working table of virtues, each flanked by the vice of too little and the vice of too much:

| Deficiency (too little) | Virtue (the mean) | Excess (too much) | Category |
|---|---|---|---|
| Corrupt | Honest | Legalistic | Integrity |
| Foolish | Discerning | Judgmental | Discernment |
| Selfish | Loving | Enabling | Love / Care |
| Self-abasing | Humble | Prideful | Self-regard |
| Slothful | Diligent | Overworked | Work / Industry |
| Self-indulgent | Temperate | Austere | Pleasure / Appetite |
| Cowardly | Courageous | Foolhardy | Courage |
| Stingy | Generous | Wasteful | Generosity |
| Cynical | Trusting | Naïve | Trust |
| Halting | Decisive | Impulsive | Action / Initiative |
| Deceptive | Truthful | Blunt | Honesty about Self |
| Cold | Friendly | Ingratiating | Sociability |
| Short-tempered | Patient | Indifferent | Anger / Emotion |

The point for a builder is twofold. First, **most product decisions aim at a mean instead of a maximum.** More engagement is not always better; the virtue of engagement design is temperance, the mean between exploitation and neglect. Persuasion is a mean between manipulation and passivity. Honest marketing is a mean between deception and tactless bluntness. When you find yourself maximizing a single quantity, ask which vice of excess you are approaching.

Second, and this connects Aristotle to [the Hooked loop](#hooked-engagement-or-exploitation): we become what we repeatedly do. "Excellence," in Will Durant's well-known summary of Aristotle, "is not an act, but a habit." [@durant1926philosophy] Aristotle held that character is built by habituation, by doing courageous things until courage becomes a disposition. A product that shapes a habit is therefore shaping its users' character, a little, in one direction or another. That is a serious responsibility. Aim the habits your product builds at something the user, on reflection, would choose to become.

### A directional test

The Sprint 2 framework gives you a practical way to check your aim. For the needs your product touches, ask:

- **Agency.** Does it expand what users can do and choose, or does it quietly narrow them?
- **Becoming.** Does it help them grow and become more capable, or keep them dependent and stuck?
- **Connection.** Does it strengthen real relationships, or substitute a thinner thing for them?

Not every product touches all three. The question is directional: for the needs you do touch, are you on the right side of them? A product that expands agency, supports becoming, and deepens connection is aimed well, and it tends to build lasting trust, which cheaper tactics do not.

<!-- learn -->

## Key Concepts

- **Why products fail** (CB Insights, 2026): running out of capital is how most failed startups end (70%); poor product-market fit (43%) is the most common reason the money ran out.
- **The Idea Trap**: falling in love with a solution before understanding the problem.
- **Problem vs. solution thinking, and the stranger test**: a real problem exists without your product; describe it so someone who never heard your idea would recognize it.
- **Strategy is choosing what not to do** (Michael Porter)
- **Where to play / how to win** (Roger Martin & A.G. Lafley, *Playing to Win*)
- **Create value vs. capture value, the value stick** (Adam Brandenburger & Harborne Stuart; sharpened by Peter Thiel, and by David Teece for innovators): creating value is necessary but not sufficient; capture is a separate, constrained choice.
- **Five forces as a market-power reading** (Michael Porter): how wide a share of the created value the industry lets you keep.
- **Blue ocean / value innovation** (W. Chan Kim & Renée Mauborgne): widen the band by redrawing the market boundary instead of fighting for position inside it.
- **Moats / durable advantage** (Hamilton Helmer, *7 Powers*): network effects, switching costs, scale, brand
- **DHM**: Delight, Hard to copy, Margin-enhancing (Gibson Biddle)
- **Product vision before strategy** (Marty Cagan)
- **The AI-era shift**: cheap building commoditizes features; strategy, moats, taste, and distribution are the durable advantages

- **The aim is a values question**: truth-seeking tells you what is; it does not tell you what to build.
- **Human nature cuts both ways**: the knowledge that removes friction can also engineer compulsion.
- **The reflection test**: would your user, calm and reflective, be glad you built it this way?
- **Engagement can mislead**: retention a user would disown is extraction, and does not count as success.
- **You own what your algorithm amplifies.**
- **The golden mean**: most product virtues are a mean between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency.
- **Habits build character**: a product that shapes habits is shaping who its users become.
